### **Speed to Lead SMS Agent Step by Step Guide**

![][image1]

###  **Part 1: What to gather and decide before you build**

**Accounts to create**

* Twilio account, upgraded to paid (the free trial cannot send real texts or register the sender). Costs money.  
* One Twilio phone number with a local area code for the client's region. Costs money, about a dollar a month.  
* Twilio A2P 10DLC registration (the text-sender approval). Costs money, takes one to two weeks, start this first.  
* Anthropic API account at console.anthropic.com (the agent's brain). Costs money, usage-based, pennies per conversation.  
* Railway account to host the app and the small database that remembers each conversation. Costs money, a few dollars a month.  
* Google account with a free Google Cloud project, so the app can write to the calendar. Free.  
* A webhook-capable form tool (Tally or Fillout) if the client's current form cannot send a webhook. Free tier is fine.  
* GitHub account, because Claude Code saves the project there and Railway deploys from it. Free.

**Keys and credentials to collect** (you will paste these in when asked, never post them publicly)

* Twilio Account SID and Auth Token, from the Twilio console home page.  
* Your Twilio phone number, written like \+15595551234.  
* Anthropic API key, starts with sk-ant-, created in the Anthropic console.  
* Google service account JSON key file, a small file the Google project generates for you.  
* The Google Calendar ID you want appointments written into, found in that calendar's settings.  
* A webhook secret you invent (any long random string), to stop strangers posting fake leads.  
* The client owner's cell number for emergency alerts, in \+1 format.

**Info to get from the business**

* The exact business name as it should read in texts, like "Comfort Pro Heating and Air."  
* The first name the texts come from, the rep persona, like "Dustin."  
* The client's legal business name, business address, website, and EIN. Needed for the text-sender registration, so this is part of the takes-days step.  
* The client's time zone, so appointments land at the right local time.  
* Business hours and which days and times can be booked.  
* How long one appointment is (for example 90 minutes) and how many can run at once.  
* The service area (zip codes or towns), so the agent can flag out-of-area requests.  
* The exact questions the agent must ask before booking (issue, urgency, address, anything else).  
* What counts as an emergency and what should happen when one is detected.  
* Whether the form already has a "you agree to be texted" consent line, or if you need to add one. Required for compliance and for the registration to pass.

By submitting this form and signing up for texts, you consent to receive text messages from  \[company  name\] at the number provided, including messages sent by the auto dialer. Consent is not a condition of purchase. Msg & data rates may apply. Msg frequency varies. Unsubscribe at any time by replying STOP to \[**702-635-9505\]** or clicking the unsubscribe link (where available), and no further messages will be sent. Reply HELP for help. See [**Privacy Policy** & **Terms**.](https://www.32degreeslv.com/privacy-policy/) 

**Decisions to make**

* Which form you are using: the client's existing one if it can send a webhook, or a new Tally or Fillout form embedded on their site.  
* Whether the agent offers a few fixed time windows or reads the live calendar for open slots. Start with fixed windows, it is simpler and more reliable.  
* The exact words of the first auto-text that goes out in seconds.  
* The exact words of the booking confirmation text.  
* Whether you still auto-reply overnight or wait until morning. Recommend still replying, since the lead expects it.  
* Whose name the accounts live under, yours or the client's. Cleaner long-term under the client, but you can start under yours and move it later.

### **Part 2: The prompt to paste into Claude Code**

I want to build a working appointment-booking text assistant. I am not highly  
technical, so I need you to act as the lead engineer and keep me on the simplest  
reliable path. Do not use fancy or trendy tools when a boring, well-documented one  
will do.

**THE GOAL**  
When someone submits a web form, the system texts that person within seconds, has a  
short back-and-forth conversation to book an appointment, and creates the appointment  
on a Google Calendar. It also recognizes an emergency and alerts the business owner  
instead of trying to handle it.

**THE STACK I WANT YOU TO USE**   
(unless you can name a clearly simpler, equally reliable  
option, in which case explain the tradeoff in one paragraph and let me choose):  
\- Node.js for the app.  
\- Railway to host the app and to host a Postgres database that remembers each  
  conversation by phone number.  
\- Twilio for sending and receiving SMS.  
\- The Anthropic API (Claude) for the conversation, using tool use / function calling  
  so the model can trigger a real booking or a real emergency alert rather than us  
  parsing its text.  
\- Google Calendar API, using a service account that the target calendar is shared with,  
  so we avoid a complicated login flow.  
\- A webhook-capable form (the client's existing form if it can post a webhook,  
  otherwise Tally or Fillout). Ask me which before assuming.

**HOW I NEED YOU TO WORK**  
\- Build in small steps, in the order below. After each step, stop. Explain in plain  
  English what you built, tell me exactly how to test it myself, tell me what a correct  
  result looks like, and wait for me to reply "go" before starting the next step.

\- Whenever you need an API key, an account, or any value from me, stop and tell me  
  precisely where to get it and what format it should be in. Do not guess or invent  
  placeholder credentials and keep going.

\- Never put secrets in the code. Use environment variables and keep a .env.example file  
  listing every variable with a short comment.

\- Flag anything that costs money or needs an approval I have to wait on, the moment it  
  comes up.

\- Keep dependencies minimal and prefer the official SDKs (twilio, @anthropic-ai/sdk,  
  googleapis). Do not add features I did not ask for.

\- Set up the project on GitHub and deploy to Railway early, so I can see it running on a  
  real URL from the start.

**BUILD ORDER (one step at a time, stop and check after each)**

Step 0\. Confirm the plan back to me, list exactly what you need from me to begin.. Stop.

Step 1\. Create the form webhook endpoint. It receives a form submission, checks a secret  
so randoms cannot fake it, and saves the lead (name, phone, issue, message) to the  
database. Give me a simple way to test it. Stop.

Step 2\. When a lead is saved, send the first outbound text via Twilio, the instant  
greeting. I will test it against my own phone. Note clearly that real sending to other  
people need the A2P registration approved first. Stop.

Step 3\. Create the inbound SMS webhook so replies come back in. Validate that the request  
is really from Twilio, and stores each message in the right conversation by phone number.  
Stop.

Step 4\. Add the Claude agent. On each inbound text, load the full conversation, send it to  
Claude with a system prompt describing the business rules and the booking goal, and give  
Claude two tools: book\_appointment and flag\_emergency. Send Claude's reply back as a text.  
Do not book or alert yet, just prove the conversation flows. Stop.

Step 5\. Wire up book\_appointment to create a real Google Calendar event, in the business's  
time zone, and to confirm the chosen time is not already taken before confirming. Start  
with a few fixed time windows rather than reading the whole calendar. Stop.

Step 6\. Wire up flag\_emergency to text the owner's number and tell the customer a person  
will call them. Stop.

Step 7\. Add the finishing pieces: the confirmation text, handling for STOP and HELP so  
people can opt out, respecting business hours, basic error handling so one failure does  
not crash everything, and a simple log I can look at to see what happened. Stop.

Start with Step 0 now. Before writing any code, confirm the plan and tell me everything  
you need from me to begin.
